mathematical_justification: All 16 parents were read. Ideal-power quotients, prime quotients, polynomial-presentation quotients, square-zero quotients, and S_q/pS_q share the additive-coset construction with induced multiplication. Well-definedness follows because changing representatives by elements of an ideal changes sums/products by elements of that ideal. This is not an additive/module quotient alone: Z/2 as an additive quotient carries no general recipe for multiplying arbitrary quotient modules; the ring construction needs multiplication on the parent and an ideal. Quotients can be nonfields (Z/4), so the existing special field k[t]/(f) for irreducible f cannot resolve this general identity. Localization inverts a multiplicative set instead of killing an ideal. However occ.39767a08c003da7e344c in formally-smooth-ring-map has a compound context: an R-algebra, square-zero ideal, quotient algebra AND canonical quotient map, described as an extension. The underlying ring quotient is a justified shared prerequisite, but a whole square-zero extension datum is not identical to a quotient-ring object. Existing aliasing is not certified as equality of those compound objects by this review.

descriptor.context: Kernel or null space of a linear map between vector spaces over a common field

form.wave2.cross107.field-vector-linear-.context: Kernel or null space of a linear map between vector spaces over a common field
form.wave2.cross107.field-vector-linear-.text: For vector spaces V,W over a common field K and a K-linear transformation T:V→W, its kernel (null space) is ker T={v∈V:T(v)=0_W}=T⁻¹({0_W}), the preimage of the zero vector in W.

descriptor.context: Kernel of a linear map between left R-modules

form.wave2.cross107.module-linear-kernel.context: Kernel of a linear map between left R-modules
form.wave2.cross107.module-linear-kernel.text: Let φ:M→N be an R-linear map between left R-modules over the same associative ring R. The kernel is ker φ=φ⁻¹({0_N})={m∈M:φ(m)=0_N}, where 0_N is the identity of the additive group of N.

descriptor.context: Set-theoretic full image of a total mapping

form.wave2.cross110.image-of-mapping.1.context: Set-theoretic full image of a total mapping
form.wave2.cross110.image-of-mapping.1.text: For a total map f:S→T, the image im(f) is {t∈T:there exists s∈S with f(s)=t}, the set of values actually attained by f.

form.wave2.cross110.image-of-mapping.2.context: Set-theoretic full image of a total mapping
form.wave2.cross110.image-of-mapping.2.text: Equivalently, for a total map f:S→T the image is f[S]={f(s):s∈S}, the direct image of the entire domain S.

descriptor.context: Foundational mapping as total single-valued assignment X→Y

form.wave2.foundation.mapping-element-as.context: Foundational mapping as total single-valued assignment X→Y
form.wave2.foundation.mapping-element-as.text: Given sets X and Y, a mapping f:X→Y assigns to every x∈X exactly one value f(x)∈Y. Equivalently, for each x∈X there exists a unique y∈Y that the assignment associates with x.

descriptor.context: Set-theoretic mapping as typed graph (X,Y,G)

form.wave2.foundation.mapping-typed-grap.text: For sets X and Y, a mapping f:X→Y can be defined as a typed relation (X,Y,G) where G⊆X×Y and, for every x∈X, there exists exactly one y∈Y with (x,y)∈G. The graph is G; X and Y are part of the mapping data.

mathematical_justification: All 14 parents were read. Formal polynomial algebras occur with one, finite, or arbitrary set-indexed variables, including S-indexed variables in the naive cotangent complex. Finite support of each polynomial does not force the whole variable family to be finite; a finite-variable specialization is not a reason to restrict the generic missing algebra to finite rank. A polynomial ring is not a degree predicate, a quotient by equations, or an evaluated element. In particular occ.aa7d5dd9a4e322c869e6 (strongly-transcendental-subring-element) has context explicitly allowing an indeterminate OR its evaluation at x∈S. Evaluation can lose information: T and 0 in R[T] have the same value at x=0 but are different formal polynomials. A polynomial-algebra prerequisite is justified for coefficient expressions, but the current mixed context must not be treated as a proof that a polynomial and its value, or a ring and one element, are the identical object. The nonzero-polynomial qualifier in the algebraic-extension source remains a source restriction, not an exclusion of zero from the polynomial algebra itself.

existing_alias_events_examined.reason: The residue field of a commutative local ring (R,m) is precisely R/m. That R/m is a field follows from maximality of m; it is not an arbitrary quotient ring and no prime localization is presumed when m is already maximal. mathematical_justification: All 11 parents were read: local/Tor/regularity criteria, fibre constructions, Henselian lifting, fibrewise maps, relative assassin, syntomic fibres and coefficient rings. They use A/m for the specified commutative local ring, including A=R_p and scheme local rings. For a proper maximal ideal m in a unital commutative A, a∉m gives (a)+m=A, so ra+b=1 for some b∈m; [r] inverts [a]. Thus A/m is a field, but a bare field definition does not specify its quotient construction, map or relation to (A,m). Generic quotient rings need not be fields, and Frac(D) preserves an embedded domain instead of killing a maximal ideal. For A=Z_(p), its residue field has characteristic p while Frac(A)=Q has characteristic zero, disproving a general residue/fraction-field identification. In coefficient-ring contexts an induced residue-field isomorphism is a map between such fields, not the residue field itself.

form.f0d993a60533fc99.groupoid-valued-pr.text: A (strict) groupoid-valued presheaf on a category C is a functor F:C^op→Groupoids, assigning a groupoid F(U) to every object U and a pullback functor f*:F(U)→F(V) to each arrow f:V→U. Pullbacks preserve identities and compose strictly: (f∘g)*=g*∘f*.

form.f7206eb9332b9389.category-valued-pr.text: A (strict) category-valued presheaf on a category C is a functor F:C^op→Cat (equivalently, a contravariant functor from C to Cat). It assigns a category F(U) to each object U and a pullback functor f*:F(U)→F(V) to every arrow f:V→U, with (f∘g)*=g*∘f* and (id_U)* the identity functor.

form.wave2.foundation.category-functor.text: A covariant functor F:A→B between small categories assigns to every object x of A an object F(x) of B and to every arrow f:x→y an arrow F(f):F(x)→F(y). For composable arrows f,g it satisfies F(g∘f)=F(g)∘F(f), and F(id_x)=id_{F(x)}.

form.wave2.foundation.pseudofunctor-to-s.text: A pseudofunctor P:A→C from an ordinary category A to a strict 2-category C assigns objects P(x) and 1-morphisms P(f), invertible comparison 2-cells η_x:id_{P(x)}⇒P(id_x) and κ_{g,f}:P(g∘f)⇒P(g)∘P(f), and satisfies the unit identities κ_{id_y,f}=η_y⋆id_{P(f)}, κ_{f,id_x}=id_{P(f)}⋆η_x and the associativity coherence (id_{P(h)}⋆κ_{g,f})∘κ_{h,g∘f}=(κ_{h,g}⋆id_{P(f)})∘κ_{h∘g,f} for composable f,g,h.

mathematical_justification: All 36 parents were read. Ordinary diagrams, projections and over-base functors, tensor bifunctors on product categories, exact functors, adjoint pairs, localizations and Hom/tensor functors all use ordinary covariant functor data in their correctly typed domains. A diagram I→C with small/finite I does not make C small, so it is not covered by the existing small-to-small functor definition. An inverse system is covariant on I^op; a represented presheaf is covariant C^op→Sets. In category/groupoid-valued presheaves the current source explicitly uses C^op→Cat/Groupoids with strict composition, not another contravariance on C^op. Opposite directions of the two functors in an adjunction do not make either contravariant. Tensoring maps sends g to g⊗id, and Hom_R(P,−) sends g to postcomposition, both covariantly; these actions are not merely tensor/Hom objects. Extra exactness, monoidal structure, over-base equations and pseudofunctor comparison cells remain separate. The generic strict-functor prerequisite is missing under the checked inventory; no alias to a contravariant or smallness-constrained meaning is justified.

mathematical_justification: All 11 parents were read. Finite free R^n in presentations and Lazard diagrams, arbitrary R^(I) in resolutions/direct-summand characterizations, and free modules over localized rings instantiate the same basis/direct-sum construction while preserving rank and coefficient-ring restrictions in the parent. Finite support of each vector in a direct sum does not imply the index set is finite: over a nonzero field the infinitely many standard basis vectors cannot be spanned by a finite list, whose union of supports is finite. Existing finitely generated modules need not be free (Z/2 as a Z-module has torsion), and locally free/projective modules need not be globally free: for R=k×k, eR with e=(1,0) is a finite direct summand of R and locally free with component ranks (1,0), whereas any globally free R^n has ranks (n,n). The already-adjudicated free-resolution augmentation forces its terminal module to be unital under its recorded free-module construction. No rank-finiteness, projectivity-only, or local-free meaning can resolve the missing general free module.

descriptor.context: Left R-module linear transformation

form.wave2.cross110.module-linear.text: Let R be an associative ring and M,N left R-modules. A map T:M→N is R-linear if T(m+m′)=T(m)+T(m′) for all m,m′∈M and T(rm)=rT(m) for every r∈R,m∈M.

mathematical_justification: All ten contexts use cosets of an R-submodule, with r(m+N)=rm+N well-defined because rN⊆N. I/I² and m/m² also acquire scalar actions through P/I and R/m because the ideal acts trivially on the quotient; that extra action is not a generic quotient ring or vector-space definition. Completion stages, filtration factors, and R/(a) for module length use the same module construction; a colimit additionally chooses a direct sum and relation submodule. A quotient set forgets both addition and scalar action, and the quotient-group meaning supplies no R-action. A generic quotient module has no required multiplication: for example the Z-module Z/2⊕Z/3 has no multiplication specified by its module data. Existing quotient-ring candidate requires an ideal in a parent ring, whereas M and N here need only be modules. The regular-sequence unitality exception remains governed by the adopted Chat policy. No checked existing meaning defines general module cosets with induced scalar action.

form.wave2.foundation.mapping-typed-grap.text: For sets X and Y, a mapping f:X→Y can be defined as a typed relation (X,Y,G) where G⊆X×Y and, for every x∈X, there exists exactly one y∈Y with (x,y)∈G. The graph is G; X and Y are part of the mapping data.

mathematical_justification: The eight occurrences test f(x)=f(y)⇒x=y for specified maps: evaluation, field-tensor multiplication, scalar multiplication, tensor comparisons and fibre maps. For additive maps this is equivalent to zero kernel, since f(x)=f(y) iff f(x−y)=0, but the module-kernel construction is not the general predicate. Ordinary injectivity is weaker than universal tensor injectivity: multiplication by 2 on Z is injective, while tensoring with Z/2 yields the zero map on Z/2. Thus the existing pure-monomorphism meaning is not a resolution. A map can be injective without surjectivity (inclusion {0}→{0,1}); no bijection, inverse function or categorical isomorphism follows. Field embeddings retain their ring axioms separately, and no default algebraic independence is inferred without the appropriate quantified evaluation map. No checked mapping definition supplies the missing predicate.

form.wave2.foundation.mapping-bare-graph.text: With ambient sets X and Y fixed, a graph-only mapping can be represented by a subset G⊆X×Y such that, for every x∈X, there is exactly one y∈Y with (x,y)∈G. As bare data G need not determine the codomain Y uniquely.

form.wave2.foundation.mapping-typed-grap.text: For sets X and Y, a mapping f:X→Y can be defined as a typed relation (X,Y,G) where G⊆X×Y and, for every x∈X, there exists exactly one y∈Y with (x,y)∈G. The graph is G; X and Y are part of the mapping data.

descriptor.context: Homeomorphism of arbitrary topological spaces

form.wave2.directional113.homeomorphism-.text: For topological spaces X and Y, a map f:X→Y is a homeomorphism if f is bijective, f is continuous and its inverse map f⁻¹:Y→X is continuous.
Equivalently, a bijection f:X→Y between topological spaces is a homeomorphism if for every U⊆X, U is open in X exactly when f[U] is open in Y.

form.wave2.quot119.simple-graph-isomorph.text: Let G=(V_G,E_G) and H=(V_H,E_H) be simple undirected graphs. An isomorphism is a bijection f:V_G→V_H such that for all distinct u,v∈V_G, {u,v}∈E_G if and only if {f(u),f(v)}∈E_H.

Both use precisely the general categorical isomorphism notion. The abelian-category hypotheses and source-specific canonical comparison are not assimilated into the prerequisite.

The 'scheme' source and 'affine scheme' source both invoke isomorphism of locally ringed spaces, meaning a two-sided inverse among morphisms preserving stalk-local ring structure. Scheme, affine and sheaf-local hypotheses remain in their parent definitions.

The category localization source requests invertibility of a morphism, defined by existence of an inverse g:Y→X with gf=id_X and fg=id_Y. This is precisely the categorical-isomorphism prerequisite already used in groupoids; universal localization is a distinct parent.

The affine-scheme and locally affine scheme formulations explicitly say 'isomorphic as a locally ringed space', meaning a morphism of locally ringed spaces with two-sided inverse in that category, respecting the continuous map, structure sheaves and local stalk maps. The existing generic categorical-isomorphism candidate requires f:X→Y and g:Y→X with gf=id_X and fg=id_Y, with no underlying-set bijection alone assumed. Instantiating its ambient category to locally ringed spaces gives exactly the same underlying invertibility prerequisite. This does NOT identify an arbitrary bijection or underlying topological homeomorphism with a locally ringed-space isomorphism; the category/morphism type stays explicit in the affine/scheme parent statements.

The full complete-local-ring formulation uses the canonical unital ring homomorphism R→lim_n R/m^n and requires this map to be an isomorphism. Its missing candidate explicitly requires a unital ring homomorphism having a unital ring-homomorphism inverse, not a mere bijection of underlying sets. This is exactly the generic categorical isomorphism prerequisite when the ambient category is unital commutative rings; in this category inverse arrows are ring homomorphisms. The m-adic inverse limit, topology/completion and local-ring hypotheses remain separate constraints in the parent definition, rather than being ascribed to an arbitrary categorical isomorphism.

The profinite-group parent defines its comparison as an isomorphism of topological groups G→lim_i G_i. Its candidate requires a group homomorphism which is a homeomorphism, equivalently a morphism admitting a two-sided inverse in the category TopGrp of topological groups and continuous group homomorphisms. This is the categorical-isomorphism prerequisite instantiated in TopGrp. Neither abstract group bijectivity nor plain topological homeomorphism is sufficient; group and topology compatibility remain explicitly carried by the full profinite-group parent and the context-specific source occurrence. The inverse-limit-of-finite-discrete-groups condition is not absorbed into generic isomorphism.

mathematical_justification: Each of the seven contexts requires an arrow with a two-sided inverse in its stated category: locally ringed spaces, topological groups, commutative rings, a localization, a small groupoid, or an abelian category. If g and h are both inverses, g=g(fh)=(gf)h=h, so the inverse is unique, but all structure in the ambient morphisms must remain. A bijective continuous map need not be a homeomorphism: the identity from a discrete two-point space to its indiscrete topology has no continuous inverse. Consequently a set bijection, a plain homeomorphism without group/sheaf data, and an isomorphism of graphs cannot resolve generic categorical invertibility. In the abelian-category sentence the phrase isomorphism of categorical morphisms means the comparison arrow Coim(f)→Im(f) is invertible, not an isomorphism between arrows in an arrow category. Specialized aliases are justified only as instances of this predicate with ambient category retained.

The finite-module-dimension source takes suprema of lengths of prime chains in Supp_R(M). The étale polynomial's quotient and the minimal polynomial's irreducibility are additional constraints, not part of this shared prerequisite. The integrality-of-element and integral-ring-map formulations both require a monic polynomial whose coefficients originate in R and whose evaluation in S vanishes. Saying 'coefficients in the image of R' is equivalent to evaluating a monic R[T]-polynomial under R→S; injectivity of R→S is not assumed.

Integral-element and integral-ring-map formulations use a monic polynomial to test vanishing at an element; standard étale maps and minimal polynomials also use the leading-coefficient-one predicate. The common prerequisite is being monic; satisfaction of a monic equation or étaleness is not identified.

An element integral over an ideal is tested by a positive-degree monic polynomial P(T), and étale/minimal-polynomial definitions use a univariate polynomial with leading coefficient 1. The monic predicate is shared; positive degree and coefficient conditions a_j∈I^{d-j} stay parent-specific.

mathematical_justification: All six sources require leading coefficient 1 in the commutative univariate polynomial algebra. Monicity does not imply irreducibility: T² is monic and reducible over a field; 2T+1 over Q is degree one and irreducible but not monic as written. Degree is a number attached to a nonzero polynomial, while monicity constrains a coefficient. A minimal polynomial additionally generates an evaluation kernel; étale presentation and Henselian lifting add derivative or root conditions; ideal integrality imposes d≥1 and prescribed ideal-power coefficients. For a unital coefficient map with nonzero target, a monic polynomial keeps its leading coefficient after mapping, and finitely many image coefficients may be lifted to coefficients in R; no injectivity of R→S is needed. The generic monic candidate includes constant 1, but a vanishing integrality witness in a nonzero algebra cannot be that constant; its positive-degree restriction must stay visible.

mathematical_justification: All six contexts use D(f)={p:f∉p}; D(f) is the complement of V((f)) in the prime spectrum. For a prime p, fg∉p iff f∉p and g∉p, so D(fg)=D(f)∩D(g), explaining localized overlap contexts. An idempotent e gives e(1−e)=0, forcing every prime to contain e or 1−e but not both, hence D(e)=V(1−e) is also closed. This special clopen case does not make arbitrary principal opens clopen: D(2) in Spec(Z) excludes the prime (2), and its complement V(2) is not open (every basic neighborhood D(f) of (2), f odd, contains (0)). Existing Spec defines the ambient topological space, not the distinguished subset indexed by f. The associated affine scheme Spec(R_f), sections M_f, an open covering and constructible Boolean combinations are related additional constructions, not identical needed meanings.

mathematical_justification: All four contexts use a positive integer p>1 with no positive divisors other than 1,p. Positive-natural versus integer terminology yields the same selected values; it does not include 0,1 or negative associates. The generic prime-element meaning in an integral domain is not identical: −2 is a prime element of Z but is not a positive prime integer, and arbitrary domains have different elements. A prime ideal such as (2) is a subset, not the integer 2. A prime power is not necessarily prime (4=2²). Field characteristic is an invariant that may be zero, not this integer predicate: if its least positive n were composite ab with 1<a,b<n then (a1)(b1)=0 with both factors nonzero, contradicting field axioms. This justifies why positive characteristics use integer primes, without declaring all fields finite. In a Cohen ring the prime is interpreted via p↦p1_R and ideal generation is separate.

existing_alias_events_examined.reason: Noetherian modules and Noetherian rings both invoke existence of an inclusion-maximal member of every nonempty poset family of respectively submodules or ideals. The abstract maximal-versus-greatest predicate is the same; the eligible family type and Noetherian properties are not identical.

The irreducible-component definition picks an inclusion-maximal irreducible subset among all irreducible subsets of X. The Noetherian ideal/module sources use the same order-theoretic maximal-member predicate in families ordered by inclusion. Irreducibility and Noetherianity are distinct properties.

The connected-component source selects a connected subset C inclusion-maximal among connected subsets of X. That is the ordinary poset definition of maximal element of a specified family of subsets under inclusion: no distinct admissible member properly contains C. The condition that the family consists of connected subsets remains essential and is not promoted to arbitrary maximality; maximal is not greatest or path-connected.

mathematical_justification: All four parents require an admissible member with no strictly larger admissible member in a specified family. This does not mean a greatest member: in the family {{0},{1}} both are maximal and neither contains the other. In the family of ideals {(2),(3)} of Z both are inclusion-maximal, even though a larger ideal (1) exists outside that chosen family. Thus the existing maximal-ideal meaning, which requires properness and maximality among all proper ideals, is not the generic family-relative predicate. Connected and irreducible components restrict admissibility to connected/irreducible subsets; in a discrete two-point space both singleton connected components are maximal, with no greatest connected subset. Noetherian formulations assert existence in EVERY nonempty family, a quantified property stronger than merely defining maximality; an empty family has no member. The subset and poset meanings supply the order but not the generic maximal-member predicate.

form.702f390cae5f9540.equalizer-category.text: Given parallel morphisms f,g:X⇉Y in a category C, an equalizer is a morphism e:E→X such that f∘e=g∘e and any h:Z→X satisfying f∘h=g∘h factors uniquely through e.

form.ce0580b5d7dc0b7c.coequalizer-catego.text: For parallel arrows f,g:X⇉Y in a category C, a coequalizer is a morphism q:Y→Q with qf=qg such that every h:Y→Z satisfying hf=hg factors uniquely as h=u q for a morphism u:Q→Z.

existing_alias_events_examined.reason: The monomorphism source requires a,b:W→X with the same source and target; equalizer and coequalizer sources use f,g:X→Y. Both require exactly a parallel pair of arrows in one category, with no invertibility or equality assumption.

The filtered-category source requires a pair of parallel arrows u,v:i⇉j that become equal after an outgoing morphism, and the equalizer source starts with parallel f,g:X⇉Y. They both use the same typed notion: two arrows with exactly matching source and target. Subsequent equalizing maps and respective universal properties remain different.

mathematical_justification: All four parents require two arrows in the same category with exactly the same source and target; the arrows are not required distinct or equal. Equalizers precompose e into their common source; coequalizers and filteredness postcompose out of their common target. These different directions do not alter the parallel-pair type. A composable pair f:X→Y,g:Y→Z is generally not parallel, and a bare ordered pair carries no equal-source/target constraints. Parallelism does not assert the equalizing equation: in Sets the two distinct maps from a singleton to a two-element set are parallel but unequal. Monicity universally tests cancellation on every such pair a,b:W→X; the pair itself is not monicity or an equalizer, and filteredness need not supply a universal coequalizer. Existing category, ordered-pair, limit and colimit meanings package different data or properties rather than this typed diagram prerequisite.
